en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Power of Psychic Faculties.
3. The Question of Devadatta’s Ordination “Venerable Nāgasena, by whom was Devadatta ordained?
“Great King, these six noble youths—Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta—[were ordained together].”
“Both Devadatta and Upāli Kappaka, the seventh, went forth following the Blessed One when the Teacher had attained full enlightenment—
bringing joy to the Śākya clan— and the Blessed One ordained them.
“But, Bhante, did not the Saṅgha become split by Devadatta after he had gone forth?”
“Yes, great king, it was Devadatta who, having gone forth, split the Saṅgha;
a householder does not split the Saṅgha, nor does a bhikkhunī, nor a female trainee, nor a male novice, nor a female novice split the Saṅgha;
rather, it is a bhikkhu who is of regular standing, belonging to the same community, and staying within the same boundary, who splits the Saṅgha.”
“Venerable sir, what kind of kamma does a person who causes a schism in the Saṅgha experience?
“Great King, he experiences a kamma that lasts for an eon.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, did the Buddha know: ‘Devadatta, having gone forth, will cause a schism in the Saṅgha; having caused a schism in the Saṅgha, he will burn in hell for an eon’?”
“Yes, Great King, the Tathāgata knows: ‘Devadatta, having gone forth, will split the Saṅgha; having split the Saṅgha, he will burn in hell for an eon.
“If, venerable Nāgasena, the Buddha knows: ‘Devadatta, having gone forth, will split the Saṅgha;
having split the Saṅgha, he will burn in hell for an eon,’ then, venerable Nāgasena, the Buddha must be compassionate.”
The statement that "the Compassionate One, seeking the welfare of all beings, removes what is harmful and bestows what is beneficial" is false.
If he ordained someone without knowing [their nature], then by that fact the Buddha is not omniscient. This too is a dilemma presented to you;
unravel this great tangle, shatter the calumny of others, for in the future there will be those equal to you.
“Wise bhikkhus will become rare; show your power in this matter.

“The Blessed One, Great King, is compassionate and all-knowing. Out of compassion, Great King, the Blessed One, surveying Devadatta’s destiny with his omniscient knowledge, saw that Devadatta had accumulated karma leading to the lower realms for many hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons.”
Seeing him going from hell to hell and from the states of ruin to the states of ruin, the Blessed One, knowing this with his knowledge of omniscience, thought:
"Although this man has performed boundless karma, because he has gone forth in my teaching, it will become limited;
by comparison with what preceded it, his suffering will become limited. Yet, even had this foolish man not gone forth..."
“Thinking, ‘He will perform an action that endures for an eon,’ he ordained Devadatta out of compassion.

“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, the Buddha strikes and then smears with oil; he causes one to fall over a precipice and then offers a hand; he kills and then seeks life—since he first inflicts suffering and afterwards bestows happiness.
“Great King, the Tathāgata does indeed strike beings for their welfare, and he does indeed cause beings to fall for their welfare.”
The Tathāgata, O Great King, brings about the welfare of beings even by killing them; having killed them, he brings about their welfare alone;
having cast them down, he brings about their welfare alone; even by causing them to die, he brings about their welfare alone.
Just as, O Great King, parents—even by killing or casting down [their children]—bring about their welfare alone.
In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata may strike beings for their benefit, he may cause them to fall for their benefit, and he may even kill them for their benefit.
Having struck them, Great King, the Tathāgata brings about only their welfare;
having caused them to fall, he brings about only their welfare; and having killed them, he brings about only their welfare.
He provides [benefit] by whatever means leads to the increase of the virtues of sentient beings; by those very means, he provides only what is beneficial for all beings.

Great King, had Devadatta not gone forth, but remained a householder, he would have committed much evil karma leading to hell, and for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, he would have gone from hell to hell, from ruin to ruin.
While traveling, he will experience much suffering; knowing this, the Blessed One ordained Devadatta out of compassion,
thinking, "For one who has gone forth in my teaching, suffering shall be brought to its limit," and thus, out of compassion, he made the grave offense light.
Or again, great king, just as a powerful man, by means of his own wealth, fame, glory, and strength of kinship, might—
through his own extensive influence and capability— lighten a heavy punishment being borne by a kinsman or a friend of his who was held in high regard by the king.

In the same way, Great King, the Blessed One, having ordained Devadatta—who was to experience suffering for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons—made that heavy suffering light through the power of his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, strength, and mastery.
Or just as, Great King, a skilled physician and surgeon makes a heavy disease light by the power of potent medicine;
even so, Great King, did he make Devadatta’s suffering light, which was to be experienced for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons.
“The Blessed One, through his knowledge of diseases, having ordained Devadatta, and by the power of his compassion and the strength of the medicine of the firm Dhamma, made heavy suffering light.
Would that Blessed One, O Great King, by making Devadatta—who was destined for much suffering—experience little suffering, incur any demerit?
“Not at all, venerable sir; he would not incur even so much as a hair’s breadth of demerit.”
“Great King, you should also accept this reason for the purpose it serves, by which reason the Blessed One gave Devadatta the going-forth.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to another, further reason why the Blessed One gave Devadatta the going-forth.
Just as, Great King, they might seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to the king, saying: ‘Sire, this is a thief, a wrongdoer; inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish.’”
The king might say to him: "In that case, my good man, take this thief out of the city, lead him to the place of execution, and cut off his head.
Responding, "Yes, Your Majesty," they would take him out of the city and lead him to the place of execution.
Then some man, who had received a boon from the king, who possessed wealth and property, and whose word was authoritative, might see him.
Being one who acts out of strength and resolve, he, having felt compassion for him, would say to those men: "Enough, sirs!
Why do you need to cut off his head? In that case, sirs, cut off either his hand or his foot and spare his life;
I myself will give an answer to the king on his behalf."
“By the word of that powerful man, they might cut off the hand or the foot of that thief and yet preserve his life.
Would that man, O Great King, acting in this way, be one who has done what was required for that thief?
“He would be a giver of life to that thief, venerable sir; when life has been given, what indeed could be said of him as not having done [what was required]?”
“But would one incur any demerit through that feeling which arises when hands and feet are cut off?
“By his own deed, venerable sir, the thief experiences that painful feeling; but the man who grants him his life would not incur any demerit.
“In the same way, great king, the Blessed One ordained Devadatta out of compassion, thinking: ‘For one who has gone forth in my teaching, suffering shall have its limit.’”
And the suffering brought about by limits, O Great King, was experienced by Devadatta at the time of his death:
"With these bones [I shall worship] that Supreme Person,
the God beyond gods, the Charioteer who tames men."
‘With all-seeing eyes and the marks of a hundred merits,
I go for refuge to the Buddha with my very life.
Thus he went for refuge as long as life lasts.

“Devadatta, O Great King, when the aeon was divided into six parts and the first part had passed, he split the Saṅgha; having burned in hell for five parts, and being released from there, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara.
Would the Blessed One, O Great King, by acting in this way, be doing what is beneficial for Devadatta?

“He is all-giving, venerable Nāgasena, regarding Devadatta. Since the Tathāgata will cause Devadatta to attain the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, what indeed has the Tathāgata not done for Devadatta?”
“But, Great King, when Devadatta, having split the Saṅgha, experiences painful feelings in hell, would the Blessed One incur any demerit on that account?
“Certainly not, venerable sir; it is by his own doing, venerable sir, that Devadatta burns in hell for an eon. The Teacher, who brings an end to suffering, incurs no demerit whatsoever.
“Great King, you should also accept this reason according to its meaning: the reason why the Blessed One gave Devadatta the going-forth.”
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why the Blessed One ordained Devadatta. Just as, Great King,
a skilled physician or surgeon [treats] a wound that has been afflicted by wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, seasonal changes, improper conduct, or external trauma—
a wound covered with the foul stench of putrid matter, containing an internal splinter, hollowed out, and filled with pus and blood—
Having healed the opening of the wound, he anoints it with a medicine that is harsh, sharp, caustic, and pungent in order to bring it to suppuration;
once it has suppurated and reached a state of softness, he cuts it open with a knife and cauterizes it with a probe;
when it has been cauterized, he applies caustic salt and anoints it with medicine for the purpose of healing the wound and for the patient’s recovery from illness. Furthermore—
“Now, Great King, does that physician and surgeon anoint with medicine, cut with a knife, cauterize with a probe, and administer alkaline salt while harboring a mind of ill-will?
“No indeed, venerable sir; he performs those actions with a mind of benevolence, desiring their well-being.”
“But would that physician-surgeon incur any demerit on account of the painful sensation that arose in him through performing the medical treatment?

“With a benevolent mind, venerable sir, and desiring his well-being, the physician-surgeon performs those treatments; how could he incur demerit on that account? Venerable sir, that physician-surgeon goes to heaven.
“In the same way, great king, out of compassion and for the sake of liberation from suffering, the Blessed One ordained Devadatta.”
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why the Blessed One ordained Devadatta.
Just as if, Great King, a man were pierced by a thorn, and then another man, desiring his welfare and seeking his well-being,
were to cut away the thorn from all sides with a sharp thorn or the point of a blade, while it was still dripping—
“Suppose, great king, one were to extract that thorn with blood; would that person, O great king, be wishing for harm when extracting that thorn?
“No indeed, venerable sir. That person, venerable sir, is wishing for welfare; wishing for safety, he extracts that thorn.
For if, venerable sir, he did not extract that thorn, he would meet death because of it, or suffering amounting to death.”
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata ordained Devadatta out of compassion for his liberation from suffering.
If, Great King, the Blessed One had not ordained Devadatta, Devadatta would have been roasted in hell through the succession of existences for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons.
“Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata caused Devadatta, who was going with the stream, to go against the stream; he caused him, who had entered upon a wrong path, [to find the right one].”
"He set Devadatta upon the path; he gave support to Devadatta when he was falling over a precipice;
the Tathāgata raised up Devadatta when he had fallen into uneven ground.
These reasons and these causes, venerable Nāgasena, cannot be demonstrated by anyone else except for a wise man such as yourself."
The third question: On the going forth of Devadatta.
